newsitem.title: TURKEY: FEATURE-Turks clash over Islamic education.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Turks clash over Islamic education.

text.p: Girls in headscarves, separated from male pupils, study religion alongside chemistry, maths and literature in one of Turkey's state Islamic schools, now at the centre of a power struggle between Islamists and secularists.

"Is there a need for the Prophet's words besides those of Allah on the walls of mosques?" a headscarf-covered girl questions her teacher at one of these "Imam Hatip" schools, located in a run-down district on the outskirts of Ankara.

Boys played basketball in the stony playground of the school of two battered grey buildings. One of the four-storey buildings was exclusively for girls, with a special section for them to pray on the top floor.
The ever-present picture of Kemal Ataturk, founder of secular Turkey in 1923, betrays state control over the establishment.

The state-run Imam Hatip secondary schools have been around since 1949, and Turkey's Islamists, who took power for the first time with Necmettin Erbakan's Welfare Party in June, have been subtly promoting them as places to prepare their followers for key administrative posts.
"There were two ways for (Islamic) conquest...weapons and education. We have the opportunity to use the second," Welfare MP Hasan Huseyin Ceylan said in a speech to the party faithful.

Ceylan said 116 of every 140 pupils to register at politics and law departments of Turkish universities this year were from Imam Hatip schools. It was not possible to independently confirm his claims.
Ceylan's assertions have worried Turkey's vehement secularists -- including the army, seen by many as the bastion of the secular state.

"Those who desire an Islamic administration in Turkey use Imam-Hatip schools as a base. Teenagers are growing up as militants," said Mustafa Gazalci, a former leftist MP in the 99 percent Moslem but officially secular country.
STEPPING-STONE TO POLITICS

Imam Hatip schools, which provide seven years' education to the children of the religiously-minded after primary school, are seen as tools to bring up Moslem "hodjas", or teachers, to carry out Islamic religious services for the public.

But many current mayors, provincial governors, local officals and leading members of the Welfare Party -- senior coalition partners -- are Imam Hatip graduates. The roll of honour includes State Minister Abdullah Gul, a close aide of premier Erbakan, and Istanbul's mayor, Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

"Families who prefer these schools mostly do not want their children to become an imam, preacher or a Koran teacher but wish them to have an Islamic identity when they grow up," Ebubekir Akkaymak of the pro-Islamist Yeni Safak newspaper told Reuters.
"The demand for Imam Hatip schools is growing every day," Akkaymak said.
Education ministry figures show around 493,000 students were registered in 1996 at 561 Imam Hatip schools. In 1995 there were 479,000 students in the 448 Imam Hatip, the ministry said.
That marks an apparent sharp increase since 1975, when published data suggests fewer than 150,000 Imam Hatip students.
But Islamists still have a fight on their hands to have the schools' graduates accepted in the powerful military.
BARRED FROM MILITARY CAREER

Imam Hatip graduates won acceptance in Turkish universities in 1974, but have so far failed to secure permission to enter military schools, which supply the powerful army that has staged three coups since the founding of the republic in 1923.
"If Imam Hatip's graduates could have entered the military schools, the world would have been different," said Ceylan, an Imam Hatip graduate and once an aspiring air force pilot.

Conservative Defence Minister Turhan Tayan recently spoke out at a parliament commission against the Islamists' demands, saying that military schools give a technical and scientific education that Imam Hatip graduates were not trained for.
"It is not possible to take in those who demand acceptance for religious and political reasons to military schools," Tayan said, referring to Imam Hatip graduates.
The army, which operates with strictly secular rules, often throws out members who are seen to be excessively religious.
In the Imam Hatip schools, children aged between 12 and 18 and mostly from religious families, learn the Koran, the life of the Prophet Mohammad and classical Arabic, and pray regularly.

Boys wear a uniform similar to secular schools, but girls generally wear headscarves and loose overcoats, covering their bodies and heads in the Islamist manner. Headscarves are banned for girls in ordinary state schools.
But despite the leniency in dress and their use as a springboard for future Islamist politicians, some say the schools still allow the state to keep Islam in check.
Although they were built with money from devout citizens, Imam Hatips are run by the education ministry and the government controls the number of pupils and the curriculum.

"These schools were not allowed to satisfy peoples' religious demands. They have been used to provide a control mechanism to the state against outlawed religious education," said the director of one of Ankara's Imam Hatip schools, who asked to remain anonymous.
